chapter: Trio, Eckstine accompanist and Illinois Jacquet, 1945-48
title: Eckstine as an artist, and why he had to leave for his family
summary: He credits Eckstine and Sarah Vaughan as literate singers, notes Billy's solfeggio, and says he left only to feed his wife and two children.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Working with Billy, as far as playing, is a pleasure, because the guy is quite an artist, he knows what he's doing. And I give him a lot of credit, along with Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker and them, for some of the things that I learned from him as an accompanist and about music. Billy and Sarah Vaughan are the two most literate singers that I've worked with, in the sense that they both read music, they know what they're doing, they know the art of singing, and the whole bit.

Billy Eckstine used to amaze me. At times he'd just do it as a fun thing. He'd sing some of the Bop tunes in solfeggio. His mother taught him solfeggio when he was a kid, you know. Then he could sing "do-me-so-me-do" faster than a lot of those guys can play it, right off the top of his head, like that.
So my leaving him was no reflection on his art at all.
It was the fact that I had a family, and I had a wife and two children, and I had to have something that I could take home to pay the rent and the food thing.
